chunks: "Atomic layer deposition is a way of growing thin films one atomic layer at a time.
Instead of flowing all the reactants in at once like CVD, you pulse two reactants alternately, with a purge in between. Take aluminium oxide.
First you pulse trimethylaluminium, TMA. It reacts with the hydroxyl groups on the surface until every site is used up, and then it stops, because it can't react with itself.
You purge the excess gas, then pulse water, which reacts with the methyl groups on the surface and re-forms hydroxyls, again until all sites are used. Purge again.
That's one cycle and it adds roughly one angstrom, about a tenth of a nanometre. You repeat it as many times as you need, so ten nanometres is about a hundred cycles.
The reason it matters is control and conformality.

Thickness is set by the number of cycles, not by time and flux, so it's extremely uniform and precise, and because the reaction happens on every exposed surface, it coats tall, narrow structures like fins and deep trenches evenly, which CVD and sputtering can't.
It's used for high-k gate dielectrics like hafnium oxide, spacers, DRAM capacitors and barrier layers.
The downside is speed: one cycle per few seconds at about a tenth of a nanometre means it's only practical for thin films."
